In fact, the authors suggested that grouping humans with similar trusting behaviors could reduce the amount of individualized training data required (Xu and Dudek, 2015).

We address the tradeoff between completely generalized or individualized models of human trust behavior by using model-based clustering methods to identify dominant behavioral dynamics among a large population. The resulting two clustered models presented here capture key differences in human trust dynamics during their interactions with an automated decision aid, and their solutions suggest different control policies toward adaptive transparency for different humans in a reconnaissance mission context. We further support the existence of the resulting models with literature from behavioral psychology.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe the human subject study used to gather training data as well as the POMDP model structure used to model human behavior. In Section 3, we show the process of applying a model-based clustering algorithm to generate clustered POMDP models. Next, in Section 4, we present the results of the clustering algorithm followed by a comparison of the clustered models, their policies, and underlying behaviors. Concluding remarks are given in Section 5.

## 2. BACKGROUND

In this section, we describe the POMDP model structure designed for modeling human trust-workload dynamics and the human subject study used to collect training data.

## 2.1 POMDP Model Description

The POMDP model for capturing the dynamics of human trust and workload behavior defined in Akash et al. $( 2 0 1 9 \mathrm { a , } \mathrm { b } )$ is as follows. The set of states $\mathcal { S }$ is defined as tuples containing the Trust state $s _ { T }$ and the Workload state $s _ { W } ,   \mathrm { i . e . , }   s = [ s _ { T } , s _ { W } ]$ . Here,

$$
\begin{array}{c} s _ {T} \in \{\text {Low Trust} T _ {\downarrow}, \text {High Trust} T _ {\uparrow} \} \text {and} \\ s _ {W} \in \{\text {Low Workload} W _ {\downarrow}, \text {High Workload} W _ {\uparrow} \} \end{array}
$$

The set of actions A is defined as the characteristics of the system recommendation and consists of tuples containing the Recommendation of the automation $a _ { S _ { A } } ,$ Experience $a _ { E }$ that depends on the reliability of the last recommendation, and Transparency $a _ { \tau } , \mathrm { ~ i . e . , ~ } a =$ $[ a _ { S _ { A } } , a _ { E } , a _ { \tau } ]$ . Here,

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {S _ {A}} \in \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text {Stimulus Absent} S _ {A} ^ {-}, \\ \text {Stimulus Present} S _ {A} ^ {+} \end{array} \right\}, \\ a _ {E} \in \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text {Faulty Last Experience} E ^ {-}, \\ \text {Reliable Last Experience} E ^ {+} \end{array} \right\}, \text {and} \\ a _ {\tau} \in \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text {Low Transparency} \tau_ {L}, \\ \text {Medium Transparency} \tau_ {M}, \\ \text {High Transparency} \tau_ {H} \end{array} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

The observable characteristics of the human’s decision are defined as a set of observations $\mathcal { O }$ consisting of tuples containing Compliance $o _ { C }$ and Response Time $o _ { R T } ; \; \mathrm { i . e . } ,$ $o = [ o _ { C } , o _ { R T } ]$ . Here,

$$
\left| \begin{array}{l} o _ {C} \in \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text {Disagree} C ^ {-}, \\ \text {Agree} C ^ {+} \end{array} \right\} \text {and} \\ o _ {R T} \in \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text {Fast Response Time} R T _ {F}, \\ \text {Medium Response Time} R T _ {M}, \\ \text {Slow Response Time} R T _ {S} \end{array} \right\}. \end{array} \right.
$$

The transition from the current state $s \in { \mathcal { S } }$ to the next state $s ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { S }$ given the action $a \in \mathcal { A }$ is characterized by the transition probability function $\mathcal { T } ( s ^ { \prime } | s , a )$ . The emission probability function ${ \mathcal { E } } ( { \dot { o } } | s )$ characterizes the likelihood of observing $o \in \mathcal { O }$ given the process is in state s.

We assume that Trust and Workload are independent, Compliance is only dependent on Trust, and Response Time is only dependent on Workload. These assumptions significantly reduce model complexity and result in independent models for trust and workload. The resulting structure of the trust-workload POMDP model is illustrated in Fig. 1. We parameterized this model structure using experimental data collected from a human subject study as described next.

## 2.2 Human Subject Study

To parameterize the human trust and workload models, we collected human subject data in a decision aid system context as described in Akash et al. (2020). The experiment captures the effects of different levels of system transparency on human trust and workload behavior and is described here briefly.

We performed a virtual study asking participants to interact with a series of three reconnaissance missions searching 15 buildings with assistance from a decision aid robot. For each building, participants chose to don Heavy or Light

Armor based on the robot’s assessment of a building’s safety. Building safety was simulated by the presence or absence of gunmen with equal probability.A search by the participant using Heavy Armor took approximately 7 seconds and avoided injury in the case that the building was unsafe. Light Armor would lead to a 3-second search time, but risked injury, which would result in a penalty of 20 seconds to recover.Participants made decisions based on the robot’s recommendations, which had a 70% accuracy in its recommendations throughout all missions. There was an equal probability of a faulty recommendation being a false positive or a false negative. An example trial is depicted in Fig. 2.

The robot used a different transparency level for each mission. Low Transparency reported only the armor recommendation and presence of gunmen. Medium Transparency also displayed a sensor bar conveying the robot’s perceived danger level. High Transparency included the features of Medium and Low Transparency with the addition of thermal images the robot captured while searching. These transparencies are study-specific, and further details can be found in Akash et al. (2020).

## 2.3 Generalized Model

We used data collected from 196 participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk (Amazon, 2005) to train the models. To create generalized models of human trust and workload, aggregated data from all participants was used to estimate the transition probability function, emission probability function, and the prior probabilities of states. For the human subject study, Stimulus Absent $S _ { A } ^ { - }$ is when the robot recommends Light Armor, and Stimulus Present $S _ { A } ^ { + }$ is when the robot recommends Heavy Armor. The sequences of action-observation data from the participants were used to estimate the parameters of each model. For model parameter estimation, we used an extended version of the Baum-Welch algorithm, typically used for hidden Markov model estimation (see Rabiner and Juang (1986) for details).

The estimated POMDP models of trust and workload are presented here. For the trust model, the initial probability of the High Trust $T _ { \uparrow }$ state is 87.16%. Note that the Low Trust $T _ { \downarrow }$ state is a complementary event of the High Trust state; therefore, the initial probability of Low Trust $T _ { \downarrow }$ can be calculated as $1 - 0.8\dot{7}16 = 12.84\%$ . The emission probability function $\mathcal { E } \left( o _ { C } | s _ { T } \right)$ and the transition probability function $\mathcal { T } ( s _ { T } ^ { \prime } | s _ { T } , \widetilde { a } )$ are represented in Table 1 and Fig. 3, respectively. Again, the probabilities of complementary events—the emission probabilities of Disagreeing $C ^ { - }$ given the state of Trust $s _ { T }$ , i.e., $\mathcal { E } \left( C ^ { - } | s _ { T } \right)$ , and the probabilities of transitioning to the state of Low Trust, i.e., $\mathcal { T } \left( T _ { \downarrow } | s _ { T } , a \right)$ can be easily calculated and therefore not shown.

These transition and emission probability functions can be used to analyze the models. For example, considering the transition probability function with the action set Light Armor Recommendation and Faulty Previous Experience $\left(  Fig.   3a  \right)$ , if the current state is Low Trust, then a Low Transparency action is approximately 25% likely to move the participant to a state of High Trust and consequently approximately 75% likely to keep them in a state of Low Trust. If the current state is High Trust, then a Low Transparency action is nearly 60% likely to keep the participant in a state of High Trust. Note that a higher bar in Fig. 3 indicates a higher likelihood of trust for a given action. Finally, based on the emission probability function shown in Table 1, an observation of Disagree is nearly 100% probable while in a state of Low Trust, while Agree is similarly probable while in a state of High Trust. For further details, refer to Akash et al. (2019a).

For the workload model, the initial probability of the High Workload $W _ { \uparrow }$ state is 66.14%. The emission probability function $\mathcal { E } \left( \dot { o _ { R T } } | s _ { W } \right)$ and the transition probability function $\mathcal { T } ( s _ { W } ^ { \prime } | s _ { W } , \dot { a } )$ are represented in Table 2 and $\operatorname { F i g . }$ 4, respectively. Further discussion of the workload model is outside this paper’s scope, as we will apply clustering to human trust models only. Unlike trust, cognitive workload has been successfully modeled for the general population using a single model (Berka et al., 2007). Moreover, it has been found that parsing visual information, such as through the human subject study’s user interface, is not a main cause of differing behaviors in individuals (Carpenter et al., 1990). Therefore, it is less likely that there are strongly-identifiable behaviors for workload discernible through clustering. Instead, the generalized workload model will be used with each of the clustered trust models to solve for optimal control policies for adaptive transparency, as discussed in Section 4.3.

## 3. CLUSTERING OF HUMAN TRUST DYNAMICS

We will now present the clustering of study participants based on their trust dynamics during the experiment described in Section 2.2.

Before describing theclustering algorithm itself, it is necessary to define the terms used. The number of clusters into which the participants are grouped is defined as $k _ { c }$ . For a given value of $k _ { c } ,$ the set of participants belonging to the $i ^ { t h }$ cluster is denoted by $m _ { i } ^ { k _ { c } ^ { - } }$ . Sets $\hat { \mathbf { \nabla } } _ { m _ { i } ^ { k _ { c } } }$ for a given $k _ { c }$ are disjoint for all $i ( m _ { i } ^ { k _ { c } } \cap m _ { j } ^ { \dot { k } _ { c } } = \varnothing \forall \dot { i } \neq j )$ .Furthermore, we obtain a POMDP model with parameters $\theta _ { i } ^ { k _ { c } }$ for each cluster $m _ { i } ^ { k _ { c } }$ using the data corresponding to that cluster’s participants. Finally, the set of models (each corresponding to a cluster) for a given value of $k _ { c }$ is denoted as $\bar { \Theta } ^ { k _ { c } }$ , i.e., $\theta _ { i } ^ { k _ { c } } \in \Theta ^ { k _ { c } }$

Algorithm 1: The algorithm used to divide the participants into a set of $k_c$ clusters based on their data. POMDP models are trained using the modified Baum-Welch algorithm as done in Akash et al. (2019a).

Result: A group of $k_c$ POMDP models.

Create $k_c$ random clusters using all participants.
repeat
    Train a set of of $k_c$ POMDP models $\Theta^{k_c}$.
    Find the log-likelihood of each participant's data using each model with parameters $\theta_i^{k_c}$ for $i \in 1, \ldots, k_c$.
    Move participants to the cluster whose model has the highest log-likelihood of observing their data given the model parameters.
until No participants are moved between clusters $\vee$ A maximum number of iterations have been completed.

We consider an adapted relocation-iteration clustering algorithm, defined in Algorithm 1, for application to the POMDP model structure described in Section 2. This algorithm has been previously applied for gene expression data (Wu et al., 2005), but this is the first instance of its application to POMDPs. It is suitable here because it clusters based on how well each model represents participants in its cluster. Therefore, participants are moved to clusters whose models better represent them until convergence is achieved. We thus extend this algorithm to the context of POMDPs.

For this paper, the algorithm is repeated for $k _ { c }   \in   [ 1 , 5 ]$ in the interest of finding the optimal number of clusters. Five is chosen as the upper bound for $k _ { c }$ to avoid potential overfitting.In order to determine the best value of $k _ { c } .$ we use the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) of a given set of clusters $\left[ \Theta ^ { k _ { c } } \right.$ , BICk . The BIC is calculated as

$$
\mathrm{BIC} _ {k _ {c}} = \ln (n) k _ {p} - 2 \ln (\hat {L})\tag{1}
$$

where ln $( \hat { L } )$ is the sum of the log-likelihoods for all models of a given cluster, and n = nmissions × ntrials $\times \; n$ participants is the total number of observations. Here, nmissions is the number of missions each participant completed (3), <sup>n</sup>trials is the number of trials per mission (15), and <sup>n</sup>participants is the number of participants analyzed (196). The parameter $k _ { p }$ defines the model size and is given by

$k _ { p } = k _ { c } \left\{ \left[ n _ { a } n _ { s } \left( n _ { s } - 1 \right) \right] + \left[ n _ { s } \left( n _ { o } - 1 \right) \right] + \left[ n _ { s } - 1 \right] \right\}$ , (2) where $n _ { a }$ is the cardinality of the action space (12), $n _ { s }$ is the number of states (2), and $n _ { o }$ is the cardinality of the observation space (2). Each term in the sum represents the number of independent parameters from the POMDP transition, emission, and initial probability functions (in that order). Multiplying this sum by the number of clusters $k _ { c }$ scales the BIC’s penalty on model size with the number of clusters. Finally, in order to determine the optimal number of clusters, the set of models $\Theta ^ { k _ { c } }$ with the minimum value of $\mathrm { B I C } _ { k _ { i } }$ is chosen. As shown in the plot of BIC values in Fig. 5, the participant population is most optimally represented by two clusters.

## 4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we present and compare the dominant behavior models resulting from the application of clustering to our human subject data.

## 4.1 Estimated Models

Here we present and define the two distinct models of trust dynamics resulting from the application of clustering to our human subject data. Note that each cluster has its own POMDP model. Each of the models resulting from the clustering analysis is distinctly different from the general model presented in Section 2.1. Here we note the dominant differences. The first cluster’s POMDP model, whose transition and emission probability functions are shown in Fig. 6 and Table 3, respectively, represents a group called the “Followers.” They have an 82.07% probability of having an initial state of High Trust.

Of the 196 participants examined, 118 were Followers. This name is chosen because this model has an emission probability function that indicates a high likelihood (32.32%) of complying (i.e., Agreeing with the robot’s Recommendation) even when in a state of Low Trust, shown in Table

3. This dynamic is not reflected in the general model that was presented in Table 1, which indicates only a 0.23% probability of complying in a state of Low Trust.

The transition and emission probability functions of the second cluster’s POMDP model are shown in Fig. 7 and Table 3, respectively. The 78 participants whose trust dynamics are captured by this model have an 84.88% probability of having an initial state of High Trust, and their emission probability function is similar to that of the general model shown in Table 1. We call these 78 individuals “Preservers,” stemming from “self-preservation,” due to their low and high trust in Light Armor and Heavy Armor Recommendations, respectively. This behavior is reflected in their transition probability function (Fig. 7). Recall that a taller bar in the transition probability diagram indicates a higher chance of moving to or remaining in a state of High Trust when presented a given action. Preservers are almost always trusting of Heavy Armor Recommendations. This dynamic, shown in Figs. 7c–7d, is similar to the trust dynamics predicted by the general model, shown in Figs. 3c–3d. Interestingly, they have a relatively low $( <   2 9 \% )$ likelihood of moving to or remaining in a state of High Trust when presented with Light Armor Recommendations, regardless of transparency, as shown in Figs. $7 { \mathrm { a } } { \mathrm { - } } 7 { \mathrm { b } }$ . This distrust of Light Armor Recommendations is not as strongly reflected in the general model, shown in Figs. 3a–3b.

## 4.2 Model Comparison

Having compared each of the clustered models against the general model, we now directly compare the clustered models against one another. Comparing the emission probability functions presented in Table 3, we see that Followers are more likely to Agree with the robot’s instructions while in a state of Low Trust than Preservers, at 31.32% and 0.08% likelihoods, respectively.

The transition probability functions of the Followers (Fig. 6) and the Preservers (Fig. 7) are also different. Comparing Fig. 6c vs. 7c and Fig. 6d vs. Fig. 7d, we see that Preservers are more likely to trust Heavy Armor Recommendations than Followers are. Preservers also react more similarly to the three transparency levels than Followers do. Comparing Fig. 6a vs. Fig. 7a and Fig. 6b vs. Fig. 7b, we see that Preservers are less likely to trust Light Armor Recommendations than Followers for all transparencies. Low Transparencies elicit an especially low probability of moving to or remaining in a state of High Trust for Preservers. The differences in the two models indicate that there exist distinct trust dynamics among the study population: “Followers” who demonstrate high Compliance with the Recommendations of the automated decision aid, and “Preservers” who make decisions aimed at minimizing personal risk. The general model is not able to capture these individual behaviors, nor does one model capture the behavior of the other.

## 4.3 Policy Comparison

These models can be used to estimate and predict the trust dynamics of individual humans. Additionally, as discussed earlier, the POMDP model structure lends itself to the synthesis of optimal control policies. Here we compare the policy designed to maximize a context-specific reward function for Followers against that synthesized for Preservers. Although their implementation is outside this paper’s scope, these policies could be used by the automated decision aid (i.e., the virtual robot) to determine the optimal transparency to use based on estimates of human trust and workload. In the context of the human subject study, picking the optimal transparency enables the automated decision aid to effectively calibrate trust so that injuries resulting from trusting the robot’s Light Armor Recommendation during a Faulty trial or distrusting a Heavy Armor Recommendation during a Reliable trial can be avoided while also minimizing workload.

A static control policy for adaptive transparency was synthesized using each POMDP model for trust, using the general workload model presented in Section 2.1 and a reward function R aimed at improving the correct decision (i.e., calibrating trust) and reducing the response time (i.e., reducing workload), specifically,

$$
\mathcal {R} = \zeta \mathcal {R} _ {T} + (1 - \zeta) \mathcal {R} _ {W}.\tag{3}
$$

Here, trust rewards $\mathcal { R } _ { T }$ penalize incorrect decisions, and workload rewards $\mathcal { R } _ { W }$ penalize longer response times, with workload penalties defined using the mean response times of Fast, Medium, and Slow Response Times. The tradeoff between $\mathcal { R } _ { T }$ and $\mathcal { R } _ { W }$ is weighted by $\zeta   =   0 . 9 1$ For further details on the specific design of the reward function considered here, as well as the associated POMDP solution, see Akash et al. (2019b, 2020). The policies for the Followers and Preservers are presented visually in Figs. 8 and 9, respectively.

Fig. 8. Follower control policy. Given probabilities of High Trust $p \left( T _ { \uparrow } \right)$ and High Workload $\bar { p } \left( W _ { \uparrow } \right)$ estimated by the POMDP model, it uses a colored transparency level $a _ { \tau }$ . The optimal policy for Followers (Fig. 8) focuses on decreasing their trust during Light Armor Recommendations, as shown in Figs. 8a and 8b. This would be accomplished by providing Followers with High Transparency when they are at risk of complying with the decision aid due to over-trust. This policy would be reversed for a Heavy Armor Recommendation and a Reliable Previous Experience (Fig. 8d). Based on the defined reward function, it is best that participants comply with Heavy Armor Recommendations, since noncompliance can lead to injury. Therefore, given the transition probability function shown in Fig. 6d, High Transparency can be used to increase trust, and Low Transparency can be used to maintain High Trust. During Heavy Armor Recommendations, Low Transparency would be applied more frequently to increase Followers’ trust, as shown in Figs. 8c and 8d. In short, transparency would be varied for the Followers to decrease trust in Light Armor Recommendations and increase trust in Heavy Armor Recommendations.

Given the differences in the trust dynamics identified in the two clusters’ models, it is not surprising that the optimal control policy for adaptive transparency for the Preserver, as shown in Fig. 9, is significantly different than that for the Followers. Unless the Recommendation is Heavy Armor with a Faulty Previous Experience (Fig. 9c), Pre-servers would always be shown Low Transparency (Figs. 9a–9b and 9d). For Heavy Armor Recommendations with a Faulty Previous Experience, based on the Preservers transition probability function (Fig. 7c), Medium Transparency is most effective at increasing trust regardless of the current state of Trust. In every other case, (Figs. 7a–7b and 7d), Low Transparency is most effective at increasing trust in Heavy Armor Recommendations and decreasing trust in Low Armor Recommendations among Preservers.

While both control policies aim to maximize the same reward function, their differences suggest that using policies customized to different trust dynamics may be more effective toward improving human-machine interaction than a single policy designed for the general population.

## 4.4 Cluster Validation

Here we verify the existence of two distinct trust dynamics among participants by evaluating underlying behavioral data to compare participant behavior directly. More specifically, it is possible to examine how frequently Followers and Preservers complied with the decision aid’s recommendation or were injured, as shown in Fig. 10. Two-sample t-tests show that there is a significant difference in the percentage of both compliant $( \tilde { t } ( 1 3 7 ) = 1 3 . 6 6 , p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ and injured $(t(189) = 6.60, p \stackrel{\frown}{<0.001})$ trials between the participants in the two clusters.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

(a) The percentage of injured trials per person in each cluster.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

(b) The percentage of compliant trials per person in each cluster.

Fig. 10. Behavioral data between participants in each cluster. Error bars are the standard error of the mean.

Figs. 10a and 10b explicitly show the expected differences in the behaviors of the two trust models. For example, as shown in Fig. 10a, Preservers were injured in a smaller percentage of trials than Followers. This is expected, given their penchant for choosing Heavy Armor, even when the decision aid’s Recommendation is to use Light Armor. Interestingly, the percentage of trials in which Followers were injured, 10.2%, is close to the percentage that full Compliance would yield—15%. The Preservers, meanwhile, were only injured in 5.8% of trials. The rates of Compliance (Fig. 10b) between the two clusters are also different. As expected, the Followers complied over 85% of the time, whereas the Preservers only complied approximately 70% of the time. These rates of Compliance are likely linked to the disparities in injury rates.

While these clusters were identified using data-driven techniques, it is important to verify these representative behaviors with cognitive and behavioral psychology literature. Prior studies of both interpersonal human trust as well as human trust in automation note the existence of distinct trust behaviors among humans. Studies using the Rotter Interpersonal Trust Scale (Rotter, 1967) have found two groups of trust behaviors: “high trusters” and “low trusters.” It was noted that the willingness to trust a novel situation is a characteristic personal to each individual. Though there were no correlations made regarding differences between humans’ trust in automation, the two groups were established through other metrics, such as high trusters being more willing to trust experimenters (Rotter, 1971, 1980). It is possible that the Followers and Preservers are coincident with high and low trusters, respectively. In the context of human-automation interaction, there have been studies examining the propensity of humans to trust automation (Merritt and Ilgen, 2008). Here, it was found that low or high propensity to trust correlated strongly to automation use. Users with a high propensity to trust had a higher rate of automation use, just as the Followers demonstrated a higher rate of compliance (Fig. 10b).

## 5. CONCLUSION

In this paper, we used a model-based clustering algorithm to identify and model the dominant dynamics of human trust in automation among a large population. In doing so, we sought to balance the tradeoffs between a single generalized, or several individualized, models of trust dynamics. Based on a BIC analysis for the number of clusters, we determined that two disparate POMDP models optimally represent the sampled population; we denoted the participants in the two clusters as “Followers” and “Preservers.” Solving each model for maximization of a context-specific reward function yielded different control policies for varying the transparency of the automated decision aid, suggesting that the use of a generalized control policy would sub-optimally calibrate human trust dynamics in the general population. Followers require a policy aimed at lowering their trust during dangerous situations, whereas the Preservers’ policy focused more on reducing cognitive workload, given their low injury rate. Furthermore, we showed that the clustered participants’ behaviors could be explained reasonably and may be coincident with established psychology of human trust. Future work will focus on validating these cluster-specific control policies in a closed-loop study.
